analysis.one_liner: Strips the EPA's power to regulate greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 255-172 on April 7, 2011, but the Senate never brought it to a vote and it died when that Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the Clean Air Act to forbid the EPA from any action on greenhouse gases to address climate change, and to erase existing EPA climate rules, including its finding that greenhouse gases endanger public health. It would also have blocked states, including California, from enforcing their own vehicle greenhouse gas standards for 2017 and later. Large emitters like coal- and gas-fired power plants would have been freed from the permitting and emissions rules the EPA had started applying to them. The bill passed the House in April 2011 but never received a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Large greenhouse gas emitters: coal- and gas-fired power plants, oil and gas producers, and big industrial facilities. The bill would have repealed the EPA rules that subjected them to Clean Air Act permitting for their carbon emissions, and would have invalidated the EPA's scientific finding that greenhouse gases endanger public health, removing the legal basis for future carbon limits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal, oil, and large industrial emitters

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the EPA from promulgating any regulation concerning, taking action relating to, or even taking into consideration greenhouse gas emissions to address climate change, and removes greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act's definition of 'air pollutant' for climate purposes.

Repeals and voids a list of existing EPA rules and actions, including the endangerment finding, the greenhouse gas 'tailoring rule' for permits, and state implementation plan actions — eliminating permitting requirements for stationary sources.

Prohibits the EPA from granting, and invalidates prior, waivers allowing states to adopt their own vehicle greenhouse gas standards for model year 2017 and later, locking in a single federal standard.

Supporters argued EPA climate rules would act as an 'energy tax' raising utility bills and costing jobs; the bill's sense-of-Congress section urges climate policies that do not hurt the economy, energy supplies, or employment.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone exposed to the effects of unchecked carbon emissions — the bill removes the federal government's main legal tool for limiting them — plus states that lose federally enforceable climate standards, and the EPA's authority to act in the future.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the EPA's 'Endangerment and Cause or Contribute Findings' — the agency's determination that greenhouse gases endanger public health and welfare — and strips the agency of any future climate authority under the Clean Air Act.
It invalidates state greenhouse gas vehicle standards for model year 2017 and later, preventing states from adopting stronger standards than the federal government.

The good-faith objection supporters raised: EPA climate permitting rules could raise compliance costs for power plants and industrial facilities, potentially raising energy prices and threatening jobs, which is why the bill was titled the 'Energy Tax Prevention Act.'

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The promised benefit — avoiding energy cost increases from EPA rules — was unproven and modest next to the cost: the bill would have eliminated the federal government's existing and future authority to limit greenhouse gases, voided the EPA's core scientific findings, and stopped states from setting stricter vehicle standards. It preserved some vehicle fuel-economy rules and monitoring programs, but its central effect was a broad regulatory carve-out for large emitters.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 255-172 in April 2011, was sent to the Senate's environment committee the next day, never got a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The House Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported on a 34-19 vote, and it was reported amended on April 1, 2011.

A Democratic motion to recommit — instructing that the bill not limit EPA's Clean Air Act authority to protect children, seniors, and people with asthma and lung disease from large polluters — failed 175-251, with 175 Democrats in favor and no Republicans.
The House passed the bill 255-172: 236 of 240 Republicans voted yes and 19 of 192 Democrats; no Republican voted no.
The Senate received the bill on April 8, 2011, read it twice, and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where no further action was ever recorded.
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, killing the bill under the Constitution's rule that legislation must pass both chambers in the same Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in the Senate, the EPA kept its existing greenhouse gas rules and its legal authority to address climate change, and states kept the option of stronger vehicle standards. The large-emitter industries that backed the bill got nothing from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The EPA and state regulators kept their authority

for.name: Fred Upton
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, held hearings and markups, and steered it through his committee to a 34-19 vote to report it amended.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after the Senate referred it on April 8, 2011, so it never reached the floor.

against.name: 172 of 192 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, and supported a motion to recommit instructing that the bill not limit EPA's authority to protect children, seniors, and people with asthma from large polluters.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor after the House passed it.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed congressional repeal of the EPA's greenhouse gas authority and issued a veto threat against the House-passed version.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost perfectly by party: 236 of 240 Republicans voted yes with zero opposed, while 172 of 192 Democrats voted no with 19 in favor.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed the EPA rules that subjected their carbon emissions to Clean Air Act permitting, sparing them compliance costs that would otherwise constrain their emissions. The avoided rules existed to limit pollution affecting the public, so their gain came directly at the public's expense.

The bill voided the endangerment finding and blocked any EPA climate action, removing the legal pathway to limits on their products' emissions. It also invalidated state vehicle greenhouse gas standards for 2017 and later, weakening demand-side pressure for efficiency.

Repealing the greenhouse gas tailoring rule and related permitting actions meant large stationary sources would no longer face Clean Air Act permit requirements for carbon emissions. Supporters argued this avoided energy cost increases; opponents noted it removed pollution limits.

The bill preserved the existing light-duty vehicle greenhouse gas and fuel-economy standards (which automakers had agreed to) while voiding California's waiver for stricter 2017-and-later standards, giving automakers a single national standard. The cost to the public is forgoing the option of stronger state-level standards.
